subject: 악보 출판과 아마추어 연주
title: Printing music for people who play at home
content: For two centuries the largest market for printed music was not professional. Households owned instruments, family members played together in the evening, and publishers built their trade on supplying them, which shaped what composers wrote far more than concert life did. The domestic market wanted particular things. Pieces had to be playable by somebody with a few years of lessons, short enough to be learned between one evening and the next, and arranged for whatever combination a household happened to own. Publishers therefore issued the same work in many versions, and orchestral music reached most listeners as an arrangement for four hands at one keyboard rather than as an orchestra. Composers wrote for this deliberately. Sets of short pieces at graded difficulty, songs with simple accompaniment, and dances in current fashion sold reliably, and several composers now remembered for large works earned their living from exactly this material. Their letters discuss what will sell in a tone no different from any other trade. The trade shaped taste in return. Amateurs learned repertoire by playing it rather than by hearing it, so a work became familiar through the hands before it was known through the ears, and audiences arriving at a concert frequently already knew the piece from their own fumbling attempts. That kind of familiarity has almost no modern equivalent. Recording ended the arrangement. Once a household could hear an orchestra without anybody playing, the reason to own the arrangement disappeared, and the market for domestic sheet music collapsed within a generation. What replaced it was listening, which is a different relation to music entirely, and the disappearance of ordinary amateur playing is among the larger changes in musical culture of the past century.

subject: 캔버스가 패널을 대신하다
title: When painters moved from wood to cloth
content: European painting was made on wooden panels for centuries before stretched cloth replaced them. The change happened over roughly a hundred years, spread from one region outward, and altered what painters could attempt in ways that go well beyond the choice of support. Panels have real virtues. A prepared wooden surface is smooth, rigid, and takes fine detail, which suits the meticulous technique that earlier painting favoured. They also have limits. Wood is heavy, it warps and splits as humidity changes, and a large picture requires joining boards, so size was constrained by what a carpenter could assemble and a wall could carry. Cloth removed those limits. A stretched canvas of enormous size weighs a fraction of the equivalent panel, it can be rolled for transport, and it can be made to almost any dimension. Painters working for patrons in distant cities could send a picture rolled in a tube rather than shipping a wooden slab, and the scale of decorative commissions grew accordingly. The surface changed the handling. Cloth has a weave that shows through thin paint, so painters either filled it with heavy preparation or exploited it, and the visible texture became part of the effect. A loaded brush behaves differently on a slightly yielding surface than on a rigid one, and the broader, more visible brushwork of later painting is inseparable from the support. Conservation inherits both sets of problems. Panels crack along the grain and require careful control of humidity; canvases sag, tear, and eventually lose their flexibility, and the adhesive attaching paint to cloth fails long before the paint itself does. Neither support is more durable in general, and the failures simply take different forms.

subject: 붙이기라는 기법
title: Sticking things onto a picture
content: Attaching material to a painted surface rather than depicting it sounds like a minor technical variation. It was treated as a decisive break when artists began doing it around 1912, and the reason is that it changes what a picture claims to be. A depicted newspaper is an illusion made of paint; an actual scrap of newspaper glued to the canvas is the thing itself. Placing the two side by side within one work forces the viewer to compare them, and the comparison is the point rather than a side effect. Painting had spent centuries perfecting illusion, and the pasted fragment declines to compete. The material carries its own meaning. A ticket, a label, or a printed advertisement arrives with associations that the artist did not make and cannot fully control, so the work absorbs content from outside itself. Artists selected such fragments carefully, and scholars have identified specific newspaper texts chosen for what they said rather than for how they looked. The technique spread rapidly and in different directions. One tradition used it to complicate the picture surface, another to make political arguments by juxtaposition, and a third to introduce chance by pasting whatever came to hand. Each treated the same operation as evidence for a different claim about art. Conservation is uncomfortable. Newsprint yellows and becomes brittle, cheap paper acidifies whatever it touches, and adhesives fail, so works made from deliberately worthless material are among the most fragile in any modern collection. Their makers frequently knew this and did not mind, which leaves conservators enforcing a permanence the artist declined to seek.

subject: 유리 제작의 비밀
title: A craft that kept its methods hidden
content: Glassmaking combines chemistry, temperature control, and speed, and for most of its history the knowledge was guarded deliberately. Workshops in several regions bound their workers by law or by contract, and the resulting secrecy shaped where the craft flourished and how slowly its methods spread. The most famous case concentrated the trade on one island, where furnaces were moved partly to reduce fire risk in the city and partly to control who could observe them. Workers were granted privileges and forbidden to leave, and those who carried the methods elsewhere were pursued. The arrangement held for generations and produced techniques that competitors could not match. The secrets were real rather than mystical. Formulas for a clear colourless glass required particular sources of ash and careful purification, and the difference between a batch that clouded and one that stayed transparent lay in proportions nobody wrote down. Colour depended on metallic additions in quantities small enough that a maker's judgment mattered more than any recipe. Working the material is where the craft lives. Molten glass must be shaped within a narrow window of temperature, so the maker works continuously, reheating and turning, and a team develops a wordless coordination because there is no time to speak. Watching such a team is watching a rehearsed sequence performed under a deadline set by physics. Industrialisation broke the secrecy without ending the craft. Machines now produce flat and container glass in volumes no workshop approached, and hand working survives for pieces where a machine has nothing to offer. The methods are published, taught in schools, and no longer guarded, and the surviving difficulty is that they still take a decade to acquire.

subject: 자개와 빛의 각도
title: Ornament that changes as you move
content: Shell inlay works differently from every other decorative material. A cut piece of mother of pearl does not have a fixed colour, since its appearance comes from light interfering within microscopic layers, so the hue shifts as the viewer moves or the light does. Designing with it means designing an effect rather than a surface. Makers control the effect through orientation. The layered structure runs in a direction, and two pieces cut from the same shell will flash at different angles depending on how they are laid, so a skilled worker arranges fragments so that parts of a design light up in sequence as a viewer passes. The pattern is therefore invisible in a photograph, which is why documentation of such work is unsatisfying. Preparation is demanding. Shell must be sawn thin, flattened, and cut to shape without cracking, then set into a recess and levelled with the surrounding surface, and the surround is frequently lacquer built up in many layers around the inlay. The two crafts developed together in several East Asian traditions and are usually practised by the same workshops. Different traditions favour different shells. The species determines thickness, colour range, and how strongly the effect appears, and regions used whatever their waters supplied, so the material identifies where a piece was made almost as reliably as its design does. Trade in shell followed, and pieces made far from any sea used imported material. What the technique finally offers is an object that cannot be seen all at once. Every position shows a different arrangement of light, and the work is complete only across a viewer's movement, which places it closer to performance than most decorative art comes.

subject: 도량형과 규격의 미
title: Why standard sizes look right
content: Paper, bricks, tiles, and books come in sizes that feel settled rather than arbitrary, and in most cases somebody chose them. Examining how those choices were made shows an interesting mixture of geometry, manufacture, and habit hardening into taste. The international paper series is the clearest case. Its proportion is chosen so that halving a sheet across its longer side produces a smaller sheet of identical proportion, which is true of exactly one ratio. That property makes scaling and folding trivial, and the whole system follows from a single geometric requirement rather than from any judgment about appearance. Other standards came from the body and the process. A brick is sized to be lifted and placed with one hand while the other holds the mortar, which fixes its length within narrow limits, and the proportion between length, width, and height follows from how bricks must overlap to bond. The familiar shape is a consequence of building rather than of design. Book formats derive from folding. A printed sheet folded once, twice, or three times yields pages of particular proportions, and the traditional names for book sizes describe the number of folds rather than any dimension. The proportions readers find comfortable are therefore the proportions that paper making and folding happened to produce. Habit completes the process. A proportion encountered constantly comes to look correct, and designers proposing alternatives report that audiences read them as errors. Several attempts to introduce more geometrically satisfying formats have failed commercially for exactly this reason, which suggests that in this domain familiarity is doing most of the work that we experience as aesthetic judgment.

subject: 포장 디자인의 설득
title: The picture on the box
content: A package is made to be seen among rivals, at a distance, for a moment, by somebody who is not looking for it. These conditions are as hard as any in visual design, and the rules that grew around them are worth a look because almost everybody meets them daily. Recognition comes before information. A shopper scanning shelves knows a familiar product by colour and shape before reading a word, so settled brands guard those two above all and change them only with great care. There are recorded cases of redesigns that improved the lettering and cost heavy sales because the look on the shelf had changed. Category conventions constrain the field. Products of one kind settle into a shared visual language — some colours mean some flavours, some finishes mean price — and a package that departs from those signs may not be seen as belonging to the kind at all. Designers therefore work within a vocabulary they did not choose, and deliberate departures are read as claims about being different. Illustration does work that photography cannot. A drawing of the contents can flatter without claiming anything you could check, and rules in several countries govern just this line, asking that serving suggestions be marked. The line between making something look appealing and misrepresenting it is drawn differently across jurisdictions. Structural design carries meaning too. Weight, the sound of an opening, and the pull of a seal all shape how a product is judged before it is used, and makers test these on purpose. A container heavier than it needs to be signals quality, which is a persuasive technique operating entirely outside anything printed on the surface.

subject: 무대 기계 장치의 역사
title: Machinery that made the impossible appear
content: Theatres have hidden machinery for as long as they have staged the supernatural, because a marvel that shows its workings is no marvel. Ancient stages had a crane for lowering a deity and a rolling platform for revealing an interior, and both devices were used so routinely that the crane gave its name to a criticism still made of weak endings. Renaissance courts then pushed the idea much further. Scene changes performed in full view became the principal attraction of certain productions, with painted flats sliding in grooves, whole sets rising through the floor, and clouds descending on winched frames. Audiences came to see these changes, and although the plays were praised, surviving accounts describe the machinery in far more detail than the drama. Therefore the nineteenth century added hydraulics and gas, and then electricity. Traps that could raise a performer through the stage in a second, revolving platforms, and elaborate flying rigs became standard equipment in commercial theatres, and the resulting spectacle drove a whole genre of production. So the technical crew grew to outnumber the cast. Naturalism then reacted against all of it. A drama set in an ordinary room requires no machinery, and the movement that demanded such rooms treated visible spectacle as evidence of an empty play. Theatres built for that repertoire dispensed with much of the equipment, and a generation of expertise was lost in several countries. Yet it returned with musical theatre and with directors who wanted such transformation back. Modern rigs are computer controlled, far safer than their predecessors, and capable of movements the older machinery could not attempt. What has not changed is the underlying appeal, which is that an audience knowing perfectly well how a trick works still responds when it is performed well.

subject: 연출가는 언제 생겼는가
title: The person who decides how a play is done
content: For most of theatre history nobody directed. The leading actor set the staging, the writer advised if present, and the company followed rules everybody knew, so a show was put together rather than thought out. The director as a separate figure with power over the whole is a late nineteenth century arrival. Several pressures made it. Staging had grown tangled enough that somebody had to bring scenery, lighting, and crowds together. Companies had stopped being standing troupes with shared habits, so those rules could no longer be taken for granted. And a new idea had appeared: that a show might carry one reading rather than merely present the text well. The first figures to claim the role worked with unusual thoroughness. Long rehearsals, settings researched from history, and crowd scenes in which every player had a named part were noted as new, and companies touring such work changed practice across Europe within twenty years. Authority followed responsibility. Once somebody answered for the whole, they gained the right to decide, and the twentieth century made directors whose readings of old plays were the reason people came. Playwrights have objected continuously, and several have written contractual protections against interpretation they did not authorise. The role varies by tradition. Companies that devise work collectively distribute it, some ensembles function without one, and opera has a persistent tension between the director and the conductor over who determines the production. What the position finally represents is a claim that a performance has an author distinct from the writer, which was not obvious before it was asserted and is not accepted everywhere now.

subject: 마임이 말 없이 하는 일
title: Telling a story with the body alone
content: Performance without speech is not merely speech removed. Traditions that developed it built a vocabulary of movement capable of carrying narrative, character, and argument, and the vocabulary had to be learned by audiences as well as by performers. The core illusions are technical achievements. Suggesting a wall, a rope, or a staircase that is not there requires the body to behave as though resistance existed, which means maintaining exact tension and stopping movement at precisely the right place. Audiences accept the object because the performer's body reports it consistently, and a single lapse destroys it. Character is built from carriage. Age, occupation, and mood are conveyed through weight distribution and the initiation of movement, and skilled performers can present several distinct people in succession without any change of costume. Training therefore concentrates on isolating parts of the body so that each can be controlled independently, which takes years. Traditions differ sharply in what they permit. One European school forbids any sound and works in whiteface, treating the form as pure movement. Others incorporate vocal effects, props, and direct address, and several Asian traditions combine stylised movement with music and text in ways that Western categories do not accommodate. The comparison is frequently made badly. Its influence exceeds its own repertoire. Physical training derived from these traditions is now standard in actor education, silent film comedians drew on them directly, and clowning in contemporary circus descends from the same sources. The form is watched less than it once was and is present in a great deal of performance that does not name it.

subject: 거리 공연의 규칙
title: Performing for people who did not come to watch
content: A street performer meets conditions that no theatre sets. Nobody has bought a ticket, the crowd may leave at any moment, rival noise cannot be held down, and payment rests wholly on what happens. The craft that grew around these conditions is exact, and although it is mostly unseen by those watching, every part of it is deliberate. Gathering such a crowd is the first task and the hardest. Players describe building a crowd from nothing over several minutes using work that is catching but unfinished, since people join a group that already stands and will not stop for one person. These ways of making a first group are passed between players and rarely written down. Holding that crowd then requires structure. A show is built as a chain of promises, each kept while a further one is opened, and the hardest trick sits at the end so that leaving early costs something. Players say plainly that this whole arrangement exists to keep people present until the moment when payment is asked for. That moment is the profession's central problem. Asking too early loses the crowd, and asking too late loses those who have drifted away, whereas asking badly makes the exchange awkward for everybody. Seasoned players handle it with a routine as rehearsed as any other part, often using humour to name the exchange openly. Regulation shapes their practice everywhere. Cities license pitches, restrict amplification, and set hours, so players compete for spots where footfall and space let a circle form. Several traditions of street performance have been effectively ended by regulation, and others have been preserved deliberately by cities that recognised what they contributed to public space.

subject: 시점의 발명
title: Deciding who sees the story
content: A narrative must be told from somewhere, and the choice of vantage determines what a reader can know. Early prose fiction used an unrestricted teller who reported anything, including what characters thought, and the more disciplined arrangements developed later as writers discovered what restriction makes possible. Limiting the vantage to one character creates suspense from ignorance. If the reader knows only what that person knows, then everything else can surprise, and the reader shares the character's misjudgements rather than watching them from above. Detective fiction depends entirely on this, and the convention that the investigator's reasoning is withheld until the end is a restriction on vantage rather than on plot. The unrestricted teller offers the opposite resource. A reader who knows what a character does not can watch them walk toward a mistake, which produces the particular tension of dramatic irony, and novels alternating between minds can show two people misreading each other with the reader seeing both. Shifting between arrangements is the most technically demanding option. A novel that moves from one consciousness to another must manage the transitions so that a reader always knows whose view they occupy, and works that fail at this are experienced as confused rather than as complex. The first person carries its own difficulty. Everything is filtered through a teller who may be mistaken, self serving, or lying, and writers exploiting that deliberately produce narrators the reader must read against. Doing so requires supplying evidence within the narration that the narrator does not notice, which is among the more difficult things prose can attempt.

subject: 필명이 하는 일
title: Publishing under a name that is not yours
content: Writers have adopted other names for as long as writing has been published, and the reasons vary enough that the practice does not have a single meaning. What a pen name accomplishes depends entirely on who is using it and what they are avoiding. Concealment of identity was frequently a matter of necessity. Writers whose work would have cost them employment, prosecution, or social standing published under invented names, and political and religious writing produced a great many such cases. The name was protection rather than presentation, and its exposure carried real consequences. Concealment of gender is a distinct case with its own history. Women publishing in periods when their work would have been read differently, or not read at all, adopted male or ambiguous names in substantial numbers, and several major novels appeared this way. Some maintained the arrangement permanently and others revealed it once established, and the choice was strategic in both directions. Separation of bodies of work is a modern motive. An author known for one kind of book who wishes to publish another may use a second name to prevent readers arriving with wrong expectations, and publishers frequently encourage this for commercial reasons. Here the name is a signal to the market rather than a disguise. Some names are collective. A pseudonym shared by several writers producing a series, or by a group making a joint statement, detaches the work from any individual entirely, and a few such names have been adopted deliberately as an argument against authorship itself. What all of these share is a recognition that a name on a cover does work, which is why removing or replacing it changes how the book is read before anybody opens it.

subject: 문학상이 만드는 정전
title: How prizes decide what gets read
content: A literary prize picks one book a year from many, and this choice has effects out of all proportion to the judgment behind it. Sales rise sharply, translation rights sell, the author's earlier work returns to print, and the book enters lists that shape reading for decades. Understanding how such decisions are made is therefore worthwhile. These juries are small and change every year. A handful of people read a submitted field within a few months, negotiate among themselves, and produce a single name, and accounts by former jurors describe compromise rather than consensus as the usual mechanism. Therefore a book that several jurors rank second often beats one that a minority ranks first. Their eligibility rules shape the field before anybody reads. Restrictions by nationality, by language, by publication date, and by publisher submission quotas determine what can win, and a small press that may submit only two titles has already made a judgment the jury never sees. Because such rules matter, several major prizes have altered them in ways that visibly changed which books appear. These effects compound. A prize winner is more likely to be taught, which produces criticism, which supports the reputation, which returns the book to further lists. Studies tracking cited works over decades show prize winners persisting far beyond comparable books that did not win, and the difference is difficult to attribute to quality alone. Although criticism of the arrangement is longstanding, it has not displaced it. Nothing else performs the function of drawing general attention to a single serious book each year, and the alternative is not a better selection mechanism but no selection at all, which would return attention to whatever publishers chose to promote.

subject: 문학 잡지와 유파
title: Where movements are actually assembled
content: Literary movements are usually named after the fact, and when their origins are traced they lead to a magazine. A small periodical published by a few people supplies what a movement needs: a place to appear, an editorial position, and a list of who belongs. Manifestos appear in such magazines because they need somewhere to appear. A declaration about what literature should now do is not a book and cannot wait for one, so it is printed alongside the work it describes, which lets readers judge the claim against the evidence immediately. Several movements consist of little more than a manifesto and two issues. Editing is the decisive activity. Somebody selects, arranges, and rejects, and the accumulated selections define a sensibility more precisely than any statement of principles could. Editors of the most influential magazines were rarely the best writers in them, and their contribution was recognising work that established publishers would not accept. The economics are brutal and always have been. Circulations are tiny, contributors are paid little or nothing, and most such magazines last a few years before money or energy runs out. Several of the most consequential lasted under a decade, which is enough time to publish a generation and no longer. Their afterlife is disproportionate. Complete runs are collected, indexed, and studied, and a magazine that sold four hundred copies becomes the primary source for a period. Digitisation has made many available, and reading a movement in its original pages — with the advertisements, the disputes, and the work that did not last — gives a considerably messier picture than any anthology assembled afterwards.

subject: 아동시의 운율
title: Verse written for people learning to speak
content: Poetry made for young children is metrically stricter than almost anything written for adults, and the strictness is functional. A child who does not yet read fluently follows a poem by its pulse, and a line that breaks the pattern loses them, so the form is a support rather than an ornament. Strong regular stress does most of the work. Verse for the very young tends toward a marked alternation that invites clapping or movement, and traditions across many languages converge on similar patterns despite having different prosodies. Children respond to the beat before they follow the sense, which is why nonsense verse works and why translation of such poems is unusually difficult. Rhyme performs a second function. A rhyming word is predictable, so a child can supply it before it arrives, and the pleasure of anticipating correctly is a large part of what such poems offer. Adults reading aloud discover this immediately when they pause before the rhyme and the child completes the line. Sound patterning beyond rhyme carries the rest. Repeated consonants, echoing vowels, and words chosen for how they feel in the mouth all give a young listener something to hold, and poets writing in this form describe choosing words by sound first and meaning second, which reverses the ordinary priority. The tradition is largely oral and much older than its printed record. Counting rhymes, skipping songs, and nonsense verses transmitted between children rather than from adults have been collected since the nineteenth century, and they show variation, regional forms, and remarkable persistence — several documented rhymes have circulated among children for over three hundred years without any adult institution preserving them.

subject: 편지로 쓴 문학
title: Novels made entirely of correspondence
content: A novel built from letters was among the earliest forms the kind took, and it ruled for several decades before being largely dropped. What this form gives and what it costs are both odd enough to explain the rise and the fall. Closeness is the main gain. A letter is written close to what it describes, by somebody who does not know what comes next, so the reader gets an account without hindsight. The writer's uncertainty, self deception, and changing judgment appear directly rather than being reported, which produces a psychological closeness that the period's alternatives could not match. Multiple correspondents supply perspective. Two people telling the same occasion differently lets a reader build what really happened from proof neither writer holds, and the best examples make this the chief pleasure. Nobody narrates; the reader assembles. The costs are equally clear. Everything must believably be written down and sent, which strains belief as events speed up, and readers saw at once that people in crisis were turning out vast heaps of letters. Satirists made this a standing joke within a generation of the form's popularity. Practical changes finished it. Cheap steady post made letters ordinary rather than notable, and the telephone took away the reason to write at all, so a form resting on letters as the natural carrier of close news lost its ground. The structure has returned in other materials. Novels built from diaries, documents, transcripts, and more recently from messages and electronic exchanges use exactly the same technique, and they inherit both its intimacy and its difficulty in accounting for why everything was recorded.

subject: 소리가 들어온 전환기
title: What happened when films began to talk
content: The addition of synchronised sound around 1927 is usually described as a technical advance. For the people working in the industry it was closer to a collapse, since it invalidated a great deal of accumulated craft within about three years and ended many careers. Camera movement stopped. Early recording equipment picked up the noise of the camera, so cameras were enclosed in soundproof boxes that could not be moved, and films made during the transition are visibly static compared with the fluid work of the preceding years. It took several years of engineering to recover the mobility that had already been achieved. Editing became constrained. Sound recorded continuously could not be cut as freely as images, so the rapid montage that silent cinema had developed became difficult, and scenes lengthened. Directors who had built their reputations on cutting found their principal technique unavailable. Performers faced a different problem. A style of acting developed for images without speech read as excessive once dialogue carried the meaning, and voices that had never mattered suddenly did. Careers ended for reasons that had nothing to do with ability, and the industry's own accounts of this period are frank about how arbitrary it was. Internationally the change was severe. Silent films crossed languages by replacing title cards; a talking film did not. Studios initially shot the same picture several times with different casts, then developed dubbing and subtitling, and the export of films became a linguistic problem that it had never been. What was gained is obvious enough that the transition was never in doubt. What was lost took decades to recover, and several critics of the period argued that an art form had been interrupted rather than improved.

subject: 화면 비율의 선택
title: Choosing the shape of the picture
content: A film has a shape before it has any content, and because that rectangle is fixed, its proportion decides what can be composed within it. These shapes have changed several times, and each change was driven by commerce as much as by any argument about art. Their earliest standard was nearly square. It suited a single figure, a face, and vertical elements, and directors composing for it used the height, so architecture, staircases, and standing figures dominate the era's compositions. Wider formats arrived in the 1950s, therefore, as an answer to television. Studios needed to offer something a domestic screen could not, so pictures became substantially wider, and marketing emphasised the difference explicitly. The wider frame suits landscape, groups, and lateral movement, and it makes a single face awkward to place, which is why the period developed conventions for composing two figures at opposite edges. Yet television then imposed the opposite pressure. Films shot wide had to be shown on a nearly square screen, and the technique developed for this scanned across the image selecting a portion, so viewers saw a moving crop chosen by somebody other than the director. Filmmakers objected loudly, and their objection is the origin of showing the full frame with black bands. Screens have since changed again, and domestic displays are now wider than the older cinema standard, which reverses the original problem. Some directors have responded by changing proportion within a single film, using a narrower frame for one period or perspective and a wider one for another, which treats the shape as expressive material rather than as a fixed container.

subject: 예고편이라는 형식
title: A short film advertising a longer one
content: A trailer is made from a film to sell it, and it has developed into a form with its own conventions, its own specialists, and an aesthetic that frequently differs sharply from the picture it advertises. The name records an accident of history, since such pieces originally ran after the feature and were moved to the front once exhibitors noticed that audiences left. The name survived the relocation, which is a small illustration of how conventions outlast their reasons. Structure is highly standardised. A typical modern example establishes a situation, introduces a complication, accelerates into a rapid sequence of images, and ends with a title, and the whole is built around musical cues that mark each transition. Audiences read this structure without instruction, and departures from it register immediately. The music is frequently not from the film. Specialist companies produce libraries of material written for exactly this purpose, and a trailer's emotional argument is carried by music the finished picture never uses, which means the advertisement can promise a tone the work does not deliver. Editing may show scenes cut differently, or shots that were removed, or in some documented cases material shot only for the trailer. The relationship to the work is therefore genuinely strange. A trailer is made from the film by people who did not make it, for a purpose the director does not control, and it is what most people will actually see. Studios test versions on audiences and choose by response, so the advertisement is shaped by measurement while the film was shaped by judgment. Several directors have made their own, and the results are usually recognisable for being less effective at selling and more honest about what the picture is.

subject: 연속극의 구조
title: Stories built to continue indefinitely
content: A running drama differs in build from any story with an ending, and because it can never close, everything about it follows from that. It must make material without closing anything, hold interest across years, and take in players who come and go, and the methods that allow this were worked out for radio and carried to television largely unchanged. Several plots running at once are its basic device. At any moment several stories stand at different stages, so one closes while another opens and a third builds, and the audience always has something nearing a peak and something just begun. A single plot could not sustain the pace without either rushing or stalling. Its community setting is not incidental either. A fixed place with many people lets figures be brought in and taken out without explaining, and ties can be reshuffled endlessly, which yields material that a story about one family would use up. Writers therefore describe this setting as a machine for making situations. Continuity is maintained by a documented history that eventually exceeds anybody's memory. Long running series employ archivists, since contradictions are caught by audiences who have followed for decades and who write to complain. Their knowledge then becomes an asset, since a nod to an event twenty years earlier rewards long attention. Absence of resolution is the form's defining constraint and its main criticism. Nothing concludes, characters do not develop toward anything final, and the moral order resets, which critics contrast unfavourably with drama that ends. Defenders reply that this form offers something else — a lasting relation with people over years — and that judging it by the standards of a closed story misdescribes what its audience values.

subject: 광고 음악의 짧은 형식
title: Writing music that lasts eight seconds
content: A short piece of music attached to a product must be recognisable, memorable, and complete within a few seconds. Composers who work in this form describe it as among the most constrained musical writing there is, since almost every resource of longer music is unavailable. Development is impossible. A theme cannot be stated, varied, and returned to within eight seconds, so the material must work on first hearing and reward repetition without any internal change. What substitutes for development is precision: an interval chosen for its distinctiveness, a rhythm that fits the syllables of a name, a final chord that feels closed. Memorability has been studied more carefully here than in most music, because the client can measure it. Pieces are tested for recall, and the findings support what composers already used — small pitch range, strong rhythmic profile, and an ending that resolves rather than trailing off. Music that fails these tests is rewritten, which is an unusually direct relationship between judgment and evidence. The form has produced material of genuine quality. Several such pieces are recognised by populations of millions decades after the campaigns ended, which is a durability that most concert music does not achieve, and composers have occasionally noted the irony. The skills transfer, and a number of film composers began here. It also raises a moral question that practitioners discuss. A piece designed to lodge in memory does so whether or not the listener wants it, and the technique works by exploiting how memory operates rather than by offering anything the listener chose. Whether that is manipulation or merely craft is argued about within the profession, and the honest answer probably depends on what the music is attached to.

subject: 머리 모양이 말하는 것
title: What people signal with their hair
content: Hair is among the few parts of the body that can be changed at will, and because it shows the change at once, it is unusually useful as a signal. Every culture has developed conventions around it, and those conventions carry information that members read without effort. Age and standing appear first, therefore. Traditions frequently mark the transition to adulthood by a change of style, distinguish married from unmarried, and reserve particular arrangements for specific ranks or occupations, so a stranger's standing can be assessed at a distance. Although such rules varied, where they were strict, breaking them was a deliberate act. Yet labour shapes practice as much as fashion does. Work requiring the head to be covered, or hair to be kept out of machinery, or a helmet to fit produces its own conventions, and much of what reads as a style choice originated as a requirement. The history of short hair among working populations follows industrial conditions closely. Political meaning attaches readily as well. Wearing hair in a way associated with a group, or refusing a style imposed by an authority, has been a recognised form of assertion in many periods, and states have legislated on the matter more often than one might expect. Regulations governing hair in schools, armies, and workplaces are contested continuously. Texture adds a dimension that varies by population. Because a dominant standard favours one texture, people with another face pressure to alter theirs, and these practices carry costs in time, money, and health. Movements asserting the acceptability of natural texture have been explicitly political for exactly this reason, and legislation addressing discrimination on this ground has been introduced in several countries recently.

subject: 식탁 예절의 기원
title: Where table manners came from
content: Rules about how to eat vary enormously and feel natural to whoever holds them. Tracing their origins shows that most began as solutions to practical problems and hardened into markers of standing long after the problem disappeared. Shared vessels explain a great deal. Where a company ate from one dish, rules about which hand to use, how far to reach, and how to take a portion prevented disputes and reduced contamination, and many surviving conventions descend directly from arrangements that individual plates made unnecessary. The rules outlasted the practice. Implements arrived unevenly. The fork was resisted for centuries in parts of Europe as an affectation, chopsticks developed alongside a cuisine of pre cut pieces, and eating with the hand remains correct in traditions with their own detailed conventions about how it is done. Each system regards the others as slightly improper, which is a reliable indicator that the rules are cultural rather than hygienic. Status did the rest. Once manners could distinguish those raised in a household from those who were not, they became a boundary, and the elaboration of European table etiquette in the early modern period coincides with a court needing ways to mark who belonged. Manuals of conduct multiplied precisely then. What such rules accomplish now is mixed. They still reduce friction among people eating together, they still mark background, and they still exclude, and the same rule may do all three simultaneously. Communities that have relaxed them report the loss of a shared framework alongside the loss of a barrier, which is the ordinary trade whenever a convention that both coordinates and sorts is abandoned.
